title: Give me yourself (Revelations 5)
hook: God, of your goodness, give me yourself; anything less isn't enough
tomorrow: when you pray, who actually starts it?

segments.voice: Clare to Agnes: a mirror that is Christ, where you study your own face to see who you're becoming. Gaze, consider, contemplate. Now an English woman holds something tiny in her hand.
screen: `GAZE INTO THE MIRROR.` → `SOMETHING TINY IN A HAND.`

segments.voice: The genie question turns up at sleepovers and in job interviews: anything you want, what do you ask for? The usual answers are money, health, more wishes. Julian of Norwich gets her own version. In chapter five of her book, she's shown something the size of a hazelnut lying in the palm of her hand. What can this be? she asks. It is all that is made, comes the answer. It lasts, she's told, because God loves it. And right after the hazelnut, she asks for exactly one thing. It sounds like it's going to be a big wish.
screen: `THE GENIE QUESTION.` → `A HAZELNUT IN HER PALM.` → `IT LASTS BECAUSE GOD LOVES IT.`

segments.voice: Here is her prayer, in Grace Warrack's old translation: "God, of Thy goodness, give me Thyself." She goes on: you are enough for me; if I ask for anything less, I'll always be wanting, but only in you I have all. The whole world is a hazelnut, small and held, and Julian doesn't ask for a bigger hazelnut. She asks for the one holding it. We look for rest in things, she says, and they're too little to give it. Christians talk about this in two ways. One side says: ask for the things. Jesus says it plainly in Matthew: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find." Bread, healing, help for someone you love. A prayer for a sick friend isn't a lesser prayer. Asking is trust, not greed, and the Lord's Prayer itself asks for daily bread. The other side says: start where Julian starts. Gifts are too small to rest in, and asking for God first keeps the gifts from becoming the point. Both sides stand on scripture, and Julian herself, a few chapters later, tells people to keep asking. Here's the thing to tell a friend: the world isn't worthless in her prayer. The hazelnut lasts because it's loved. It just isn't God.
screen: `GIVE ME THYSELF.` · `ONE VIEW: ASK, AND IT SHALL BE GIVEN.` · `THE OTHER: GIFTS ARE TOO SMALL TO REST IN.` · `LOVED, BUT NOT GOD.` · then, large: `ONLY YOU SUFFICE.`

segments.voice: Hold something small in your open palm: a coin, a key, a pebble. Let it stand for all that is made, small and held, and keep your hand open through the whole sit. If you pray, you can say Julian's own words slowly: God, of thy goodness, give me thyself.
Give me yourself. Julian of Norwich's prayer to God for God himself, because nothing less is enough, and everything else is held in him.
Your line: only you suffice. She asked for the one holding the hazelnut, not a bigger hazelnut. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Christians of many churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love, and some pray her line 'God, of thy goodness, give me thyself' as a short prayer of their own.

fork.setup: your aunt only prays 'give me yourself' and calls praying for a new job shallow. you pray for the job. what's her best case?
options: praying for things shows you don't trust God.
gifts are too small to rest in; ask for God first.

fork.reveal: that's Julian's case: only in God is everything. and your side has its own best case: ask, and it shall be given you.

what it means: Julian asks for God himself, since anything less leaves her wanting.

chat.says: is it selfish i keep praying pop's wrist heals before graduation? feels like a wish list
options: Not selfish. Jesus says ask. Julian adds: ask for the one holding it all, too.
Yes. Julian says asking God for any thing at all is greedy.
No, and skip the rest. Julian says the gifts are what prayer is for.
chat.meaning: Christians hold both: Jesus says ask, and Julian asks first for God himself, since only in God is everything.
